content.text: Firing thousands of parallel requests at the Messages API pays full price for every token and spends the same rate limits your live product depends on. When nobody is waiting on each answer, the Message Batches API is the better tool: it bills all usage at 50% of standard prices, runs under its own rate limits, and most batches finish within an hour. The trade-off is latency, so it's a fit for bulk work, not for users waiting on a reply.
The support team adopts a new ticket taxonomy and asks you to relabel last year's 40,000 tickets with Claude Opus 5.5. You write an

script with 50 concurrent requests, tuned to sit just under your organization's rate limit, and start it after lunch. By three o'clock the customer-facing support chat, running on the same model in the same organization, is answering some users with errors: 429s that weren't there in the morning. The script finishes in the evening, and the invoice shows every token at full price.
"The fastest and cheapest way to process thousands of documents is firing parallel requests as fast as rate limits allow." It's how most of us scale any API client:

items.text: More concurrency means more throughput, and the rate limit looks like the only ceiling.
The SDK already retries 429s with backoff, so pushing right up against the limit feels safe.
"Batch API" sounds like an overnight job from another era, slow by design.
A parallel script shows progress immediately, and you can stop it the moment something looks wrong.

content.text: The half-truth: for a few hundred requests that a user is waiting on, parallel calls are the right tool. For thousands of requests that nobody reads until tomorrow, they cost twice what they need to and compete with your production traffic for the same limits.
Parallel calls share everything with production

are set at the organization level and measured per model class. A bulk script and your live product calling the same model draw from the same requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute budget. Tune the script to "just under the limit" and there's nothing left for real users, and the SDK's automatic retries only add attempts. Every one of those requests is billed at the standard price: $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens on Claude Opus 5.5.
A batch is one asynchronous job

items.text: Size:
up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB per batch, whichever comes first.
Price:
all usage at 50% of standard prices, which makes Claude Opus 5.5 $2 input and $10 output per million tokens. The discount covers input, output and "any special tokens".
Time:
most batches complete within an hour. Results are available when every request has finished or after 24 hours, and requests not processed by then expire.
Limits:
batches have their own rate limits, and "Usage of the Batches API does not affect rate limits in the Messages API."
Retention:
results stay downloadable for 29 days after the batch is created.

content.text: So the honest comparison isn't "fast versus slow". It's "seconds per answer at full price, competing with production" versus "an hour or so for the whole set at half price, on separate limits". Batches can even go further than the synchronous API: with the
beta header, a batched Claude Opus 5.5 request can set
up to 300,000, where the synchronous limit is 128K.

The first version races the rate limit. The second submits one batch and goes on with the day:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import asyncio

import anthropic

client = anthropic.AsyncAnthropic()
limit = asyncio.Semaphore(50)  # tuned to sit just under our rate limit


async def label(ticket: dict) -> str:
    async with limit:
        reply = await client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=256,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt_for(ticket)}],
        )
    return next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")


async def main():
    labels = await asyncio.gather(*(label(t) for t in TICKETS))
    print(len(labels), "labels, every token at the standard price")


asyncio.run(main())

tabs.label: ✅ Right

content.text: Once the batch has ended, a second job reads the results:

blocks.code:
labels, to_fix, to_resend = {}, [], []
for item in client.messages.batches.results(BATCH_ID):
    ticket_id = item.custom_id.removeprefix("ticket-")
    result = item.result
    if result.type == "succeeded":
        blocks = result.message.content
        labels[ticket_id] = next(b.text for b in blocks if b.type == "text")
    elif result.type == "errored" and \
            result.error.error.type == "invalid_request_error":
        to_fix.append(ticket_id)  # resending it unchanged fails again
    else:  # other errors, canceled, expired: resend as they are
        to_resend.append(ticket_id)
print(len(labels), len(to_fix), len(to_resend))  # labeled, fix, resend

blocks.title: Results come back in any order

content.text: The results file is "not guaranteed to be in the same order as requests". Code that zips results with the input list by position labels the wrong tickets without raising anything. Put your own key in
(1 to 64 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores, unique within the batch) and match on it.

content.text: Batch and caching discounts combine. Put identical

blocks on the shared prefix, such as the taxonomy and instructions, in every request. Hits are best-effort because requests run concurrently; the docs report 30% to 98% depending on traffic, and suggest the 1-hour cache duration because a batch can run longer than 5 minutes.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Sort your workloads by who's waiting

content.text: Anything a user waits on stays on the Messages API. Evaluations, backfills, nightly summaries and bulk classification are batch candidates.
Send a single request through the Messages API first, as the docs suggest, so a validation error doesn't come back 100,000 times.

items.text: Parallel requests pay full price and share your organization's rate limits with production.
The Message Batches API bills all usage at 50% of standard prices and has its own rate limits.
Most batches finish within an hour, but plan for up to 24 hours: batches are for work nobody waits on.
Results arrive in any order; match them by
custom_id
, never by position.
Errored, canceled and expired requests aren't billed, but they still need your code to fix or resend them.
